The eldest son of Amram and Jochebed, a daughter of Levi ([Ex. 6:20](#Exod.6.20)). Some explain the name as meaning mountaineer, others mountain of strength, illuminator. He was born in Egypt three years before his brother Moses, and a number of years after his sister Miriam (2:1, 4; 7:7). He married Elisheba, the daughter of Amminadab of the house of Judah (6:23; [1 Chr. 2:10](#1Chr.2.10)), by whom he had four sons, Nadab and Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar. …
One of the seven eunuchs in Ahasuerus’s court ([Esther 1:10](#Esth.1.10); [2:21](#Esth.2.21)).
The father of Adoniram, whom Solomon set over the tribute ([1 Kings 4:6](#1Kgs.4.6)); i.e., the forced labour (R.V., “levy”).
Servant of God, ([Jer. 36:26](#Jer.36.26)), the father of Shelemiah.
Servant of God, ([1 Chr. 5:15](#1Chr.5.15)), a Gadite chief.
The son of Hillel, a Pirathonite, the tenth judge of Israel ([Judg. 12:13-15](#Judg.12.13)). He is probably the Bedan of [1 Sam. 12:11](#1Sam.12.11).
The first-born of Gibeon of the tribe of Benjamin ([1 Chr. 8:30](#1Chr.8.30); [9:36](#1Chr.9.36)).
One of the “sons” of Shashak ([1 Chr. 8:23](#1Chr.8.23)).

(Heb. Hebhel), a breath, or vanity, the second son of Adam and Eve. He was put to death by his brother Cain ([Gen. 4:1-16](#Gen.4.1)). Guided by the instruction of their father, the two brothers were trained in the duty of worshipping God. “And in process of time” (marg. “at the end of days”, i.e., on the Sabbath) each of them offered up to God of the first-fruits of his labours. …

The second son of Samuel ([1 Sam. 8:2](#1Sam.8.2); [1 Chr. 6:28](#1Chr.6.28)). His conduct, along with that of his brother, as a judge in Beer-sheba, to which office his father had appointed him, led to popular discontent, and ultimately provoked the people to demand a royal form of government.
One of the sons of Becher, the son of Benjamin ([1 Chr. 7:8](#1Chr.7.8)). “Abiah,” A.V.
Father of abundance, or my father excels, the son of Ahimelech the high priest. …
Or Abi’dah, father of knowledge; knowing, one of the five sons of Midian, who was the son of Abraham by Keturah ([1 Chr. 1:33](#1Chr.1.33)), and apparently the chief of an Arab tribe.
Father of judgment; judge, head of the tribe of Benjamin at the Exodus ([Num. 1:11](#Num.1.11); [2:22](#Num.2.22)).

The son of Zeror and father of Ner, who was the grandfather of Saul ([1 Sam. 14:51](#1Sam.14.51); [1 Chr. 8:33](#1Chr.8.33); [9:39](#1Chr.9.39)). In [1 Sam. 9:1](#1Sam.9.1), he is called the “father,” probably meaning the grandfather, of Kish.
An Arbathite, one of David’s warriors ([1 Chr. 11:32](#1Chr.11.32)); called also Abi-albon ([2 Sam. 23:31](#2Sam.23.31)).

The second of the three sons of Hammoleketh, the sister of Gilead. He was the grandson of Manasseh ([1 Chr. 7:18](#1Chr.7.18)). From his family Gideon sprang ([Josh. 17:2](#Josh.17.2); comp. [Judg. 6:34](#Judg.6.34); [8:2](#Judg.8.2)). He was also called Jeezer ([Num. 26:30](#Num.26.30)).
One of David’s thirty warriors ([2 Sam. 23:27](#2Sam.23.27); comp. [1 Chr. 27:12](#1Chr.27.12)).

The wife of the churlish Nabal, who dwelt in the district of Carmel ([1 Sam. 25:3](#1Sam.25.3)). She showed great prudence and delicate management at a critical period of her husband’s life. She was “a woman of good understanding, and of a beautiful countenance.” After Nabal’s death she became the wife of David ([1 Sam. 25:14-42](#1Sam.25.14)), and was his companion in all his future fortunes ([1 Sam. 27:3](#1Sam.27.3); [30:5](#1Sam.30.5); [2 Sam. 2:2](#2Sam.2.2)). By her David had a son called Chileab ([2 Sam. 3:3](#2Sam.3.3)), elsewhere called Daniel ([1 Chr. 3:1](#1Chr.3.1)).
The sister of David, and wife of Jether an Ishmaelite ([1 Chr. 2:16](#1Chr.2.16), [17](#1Chr.2.17)). She was the mother of Amasa ([2 Sam. 17:25](#2Sam.17.25)).
The father of Esther and uncle of Mordecai ([Esther 2:15](#Esth.2.15)).
The second wife of King Rehoboam ([2 Chr. 11:18](#2Chr.11.18)), a descendant of Eliab, David’s eldest brother.

Father of Him; i.e., “worshipper of God”, the second of the sons of Aaron ([Ex. 6:23](#Exod.6.23); [Num. 3:2](#Num.3.2); [26:60](#Num.26.60); [1 Chr. 6:3](#1Chr.6.3)). Along with his three brothers he was consecrated to the priest’s office ([Ex. 28:1](#Exod.28.1)). With his father and elder brother he accompanied the seventy elders part of the way up the mount with Moses ([Ex. 24:1](#Exod.24.1), [9](#Exod.24.9)). On one occasion he and Nadab his brother offered incense in their censers filled with “strange” (i.e., common) fire, i.e., not with fire taken from the great brazen altar ([Lev. 6:9](#Lev.6.9), etc.), and for this offence they were struck dead, and were taken out and buried without the camp ([Lev. 10:1-11](#Lev.10.1); comp. [Num. 3:4](#Num.3.4); [26:61](#Num.26.61); [1 Chr. 24:2](#1Chr.24.2)). It is probable that when they committed this offence they were intoxicated, for immediately after is given the law prohibiting the use of wine or strong drink to the priests.
One of the sons of Bela, the son of Benjamin ([1 Chr. 8:3](#1Chr.8.3)); called also Ahihud (ver. 7).

The son of Rehoboam, whom he succeeded on the throne of Judah ([1 Chr. 3:10](#1Chr.3.10)). He is also called Abijam ([1 Kings 14:31](#1Kgs.14.31); [15:1-8](#1Kgs.15.1)). He began his three years’ reign ([2 Chr. 12:16](#2Chr.12.16); [13:1](#2Chr.13.1), [2](#2Chr.13.2)) with a strenuous but unsuccessful effort to bring back the ten tribes to their allegiance. His address to “Jeroboam and all Israel,” before encountering them in battle, is worthy of being specially noticed ([2 Chr. 13:5-12](#2Chr.13.5)). It was a very bloody battle, no fewer than 500,000 of the army of Israel having perished on the field. …
The daughter of Zechariah ([2 Chr. 29:1](#2Chr.29.1); comp. [Isa. 8:2](#Isa.8.2)), and afterwards the wife of Ahaz. She is also called Abi ([2 Kings 18:2](#2Kgs.18.2)).

A descendant of Eleazar, the son of Aaron, a chief of one of the twenty-four orders into which the priesthood was divided by David ([1 Chr. 24:10](#1Chr.24.10)). The order of Abijah was one of those which did not return from the Captivity ([Ezra 2:36-39](#Ezra.2.36); [Neh. 7:39-42](#Neh.7.39); [12:1](#Neh.12.1)).

A son of Jeroboam, the first king of Israel. On account of his severe illness when a youth, his father sent his wife to consult the prophet Ahijah regarding his recovery. The prophet, though blind with old age, knew the wife of Jeroboam as soon as she approached, and under a divine impulse he announced to her that inasmuch as in Abijah alone of all the house of Jeroboam there was found “some good thing toward the Lord,” he only would come to his grave in peace. As his mother crossed the threshold of the door on her return, the youth died, and “all Israel mourned for him” ([1 Kings 14:1-18](#1Kgs.14.1)).
Father of Mael, one of the sons or descendants of Joktan, in Northern Arabia ([Gen. 10:28](#Gen.10.28); [1 Chr. 1:22](#1Chr.1.22)).

A son of Gideon ([Judg. 9:1](#Judg.9.1)), who was proclaimed king after the death of his father ([Judg. 8:33-9:6](#Judg.8.33)). One of his first acts was to murder his brothers, seventy in number, “on one stone,” at Ophrah. Only one named Jotham escaped. He was an unprincipled, ambitious ruler, often engaged in war with his own subjects. When engaged in reducing the town of Thebez, which had revolted, he was struck mortally on his head by a mill-stone, thrown by the hand of a woman from the wall above. Perceiving that the wound was mortal, he desired his armour-bearer to thrust him through with his sword, that it might not be said he had perished by the hand of a woman ([Judg. 9:50-57](#Judg.9.50)).

A king of Gerar in the time of Isaac, probably the son of the preceeding ([Gen. 26:1-22](#Gen.26.1)). Isaac sought refuge in his territory during a famine, and there he acted a part with reference to his wife Rebekah similar to that of his father Abraham with reference to Sarah. Abimelech rebuked him for the deception, which he accidentally discovered. Isaac settled for a while here, and prospered. Abimelech desired him, however, to leave his territory, which Isaac did. Abimelech afterwards visited him when he was encamped at Beer-sheba, and expressed a desire to renew the covenant which had been entered into between their fathers ([Gen. 26:26-31](#Gen.26.26)).
One of Saul’s sons, who peristed with his father in the battle of Gilboa ([1 Sam. 31:2](#1Sam.31.2); [1 Chr. 10:2](#1Chr.10.2)).

A Levite of Kirjath-jearim, in whose house the ark of the covenant was deposited after having been brought back from the land of the Philistines ([1 Sam. 7:1](#1Sam.7.1)). It remained there twenty years, till it was at length removed by David ([1 Sam. 7:1](#1Sam.7.1), [2](#1Sam.7.2); [1 Chr. 13:7](#1Chr.13.7)).
The second of the eight sons of Jesse ([1 Sam. 16:8](#1Sam.16.8)). He was with Saul in the campaign against the Philistines in which Goliath was slain ([1 Sam. 17:13](#1Sam.17.13)).
One of Solomon’s officers, who “provided victuals for the king and his household.” He presided, for this purpose, over the district of Dor ([1 Kings 4:11](#1Kgs.4.11)).
Father of kindness, the father of Barak ([Judg. 4:6](#Judg.4.6); [5:1](#Judg.5.1)).

One of the sons of Eliab, who joined Korah in the conspiracy against Moses and Aaron. He and all the conspirators, with their families and possessions (except the children of Korah), were swallowed up by an earthquake ([Num. 16:1-27](#Num.16.1); [26:9](#Num.26.9); [Ps. 106:17](#Ps.106.17)).
The eldest son of Hiel the Bethelite, who perished prematurely in consequence of his father’s undertaking to rebuild Jericho ([1 Kings 16:34](#1Kgs.16.34)), according to the words of Joshua (6:26).

Father of (i.e., “given to”) error, a young woman of Shunem, distinguished for her beauty. She was chosen to minister to David in his old age. She became his wife ([1 Kings 1:3](#1Kgs.1.3), [4](#1Kgs.1.4), [15](#1Kgs.1.15)). After David’s death Adonijah persuaded Bathsheba, Solomon’s mother, to entreat the king to permit him to marry Abishag. Solomon suspected in this request an aspiration to the throne, and therefore caused him to be put to death ([1 Kings 2:17-25](#1Kgs.2.17)).
Father of (i.e., “desirous of”) a gift, the eldest son of Zeruiah, David’s sister. …
The son of Phinehas the high priest ([1 Chr. 6:4](#1Chr.6.4), [5](#1Chr.6.5), [50](#1Chr.6.50); [Ezra 7:5](#Ezra.7.5)).
Father of the wall; i.e., “mason”, one of the two sons of Shammai of the tribe of Judah ([1 Chr. 2:28](#1Chr.2.28), [29](#1Chr.2.29)).
Father of dew; i.e., “fresh”, David’s fifth wife ([2 Sam. 3:4](#2Sam.3.4)).
Father of goodness, a Benjamite ([1 Chr. 8:11](#1Chr.8.11)).
A descendant of Zerubbabel and father of Eliakim ([Matt. 1:13](#Matt.1.13), “Abiud”); called also Juda ([Luke 3:26](#Luke.3.26)), and Obadiah ([1 Chr. 3:21](#1Chr.3.21)).

Father of light; i.e., “enlightening”, the son of Ner and uncle of Saul. He was commander-in-chief of Saul’s army ([1 Sam. 14:50](#1Sam.14.50); [17:55](#1Sam.17.55); [20:25](#1Sam.20.25)). He first introduced David to the court of Saul after the victory over Goliath ([1 Sam. 17:57](#1Sam.17.57)). After the death of Saul, David was made king over Judah, and reigned in Hebron. Among the other tribes there was a feeling of hostility to Judah; and Abner, at the head of Ephraim, fostered this hostility in the interest of the house of Saul, whose son Ish-bosheth he caused to be proclaimed king ([2 Sam. 2:8](#2Sam.2.8)). A state of war existed between these two kings. …

Father of a multitude, son of Terah, named ([Gen. 11:27](#Gen.11.27)) before his older brothers Nahor and Haran, because he was the heir of the promises. Till the age of seventy, Abram sojourned among his kindred in his native country of Chaldea. He then, with his father and his family and household, quitted the city of Ur, in which he had hitherto dwelt, and went some 300 miles north to Haran, where he abode fifteen years. The cause of his migration was a call from God ([Acts 7:2-4](#Acts.7.2)). There is no mention of this first call in the Old Testament; it is implied, however, in [Gen. 12](#Gen.12). While they tarried at Haran, Terah died at the age of 205 years. …

Father of peace; i.e., “peaceful” David’s son by Maacah ([2 Sam. 3:3](#2Sam.3.3); comp. [1 Kings 1:6](#1Kgs.1.6)). He was noted for his personal beauty and for the extra-ordinary profusion of the hair of his head ([2 Sam. 14:25](#2Sam.14.25),[26](#2Sam.14.26)). The first public act of his life was the blood-revenge he executed against Amnon, David’s eldest son, who had basely wronged Absalom’s sister Tamar. This revenge was executed at the time of the festivities connected with a great sheep-shearing at Baal-hazor. David’s other sons fled from the place in horror, and brought the tidings of the death of Amnon to Jerusalem. Alarmed for the consequences of the act, Absalom fled to his grandfather at Geshur, and there abode for three years ([2 Sam. 3:3](#2Sam.3.3); [13:23-38](#2Sam.13.23)).

([1 Cor. 16:17](#1Cor.16.17)), one of the members of the church of Corinth who, with Fortunatus and Stephanas, visited Paul while he was at Ephesus, for the purpose of consulting him on the affairs of the church. These three probably were the bearers of the letter from Corinth to the apostle to which he alludes in [1 Cor. 7:1](#1Cor.7.1).

Called also Achar, i.e., one who troubles ([1 Chr. 2:7](#1Chr.2.7)), in commemoration of his crime, which brought upon him an awful destruction ([Josh. 7:1](#Josh.7.1)). On the occasion of the fall of Jericho, he seized, contrary to the divine command, an ingot of gold, a quantity of silver, and a costly Babylonish garment, which he hid in his tent. Joshua was convinced that the defeat which the Israelites afterwards sustained before Ai was a proof of the divine displeasure on account of some crime, and he at once adopted means by the use of the lot for discovering the criminal. It was then found that Achan was guilty, and he was stoned to death in the valley of Achor. He and all that belonged to him were then consumed by fire, and a heap of stones was raised over the ashes.

The son of Micah, one of those whom Josiah sent to the prophetess Huldah to ascertain from her the meaning of the recently discovered book of the law ([2 Chr. 34:20](#2Chr.34.20)). He is called Achbor in [2 Kings 22:12](#2Kgs.22.12).

The king with whom David sought refuge when he fled from Saul ([1 Sam. 21:10-15](#1Sam.21.10)). He is called Abimelech in the superscription of [Ps. 34](#Ps.34). It was probably this same king to whom David a second time repaired at the head of a band of 600 warriors, and who assigned him Ziklag, whence he carried on war against the surrounding tribes ([1 Sam. 27:5-12](#1Sam.27.5)). Achish had great confidence in the valour and fidelity of David ([1 Sam. 28:1](#1Sam.28.1), [2](#1Sam.28.2)), but at the instigation of his courtiers did not permit him to go up to battle along with the Philistine hosts ([1 Sam. 29:2-11](#1Sam.29.2)). David remained with Achish a year and four months.

Anklet, Caleb’s only daughter ([1 Chr. 2:49](#1Chr.2.49)). She was offered in marriage to the man who would lead an attack on the city of Debir, or Kirjath-sepher. This was done by Othniel (q.v.), who accordingly obtained her as his wife ([Josh. 15:16-19](#Josh.15.16); [Judg. 1:9-15](#Judg.1.9)).
The first of Esau’s three wives, the daughter of Elon the Hittite ([Gen. 36:2](#Gen.36.2), [4](#Gen.36.4)), called also Bashemath (26:34).
The first of Lamech’s two wives, and the mother of Jabal and Jubal ([Gen. 4:19](#Gen.4.19), [20](#Gen.4.20), [23](#Gen.4.23)).

Red, a Babylonian word, the generic name for man, having the same meaning in the Hebrew and the Assyrian languages. It was the name given to the first man, whose creation, fall, and subsequent history and that of his descendants are detailed in the first book of Moses ([Gen. 1:27](#Gen.1.27)-ch. 5). “God created man [Heb., Adam] in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them.”
Miracle of God, the third of the twelve sons of Ishmael, and head of an Arabian tribe ([Gen. 25:13](#Gen.25.13); [1 Chr. 1:29](#1Chr.1.29)).
Ample, splendid, son of Bela ([1 Chr. 8:3](#1Chr.8.3)); called also “Ard” ([Gen. 46:21](#Gen.46.21))
Ornament, ([Luke 3:28](#Luke.3.28)), the son of Cosam, and father of Melchi, one of the progenitors of Christ.
A family head of the tribe of Simeon ([1 Chr. 4:36](#1Chr.4.36)).
Slender, one of David’s warriors ([1 Chr. 11:42](#1Chr.11.42)), a Reubenite.
The Eznite, one of David’s mighty men ([2 Sam. 23:8](#2Sam.23.8)).
A chief of the tribe of Manasseh who joined David at Ziklag ([1 Chr. 12:20](#1Chr.12.20)).
A general under Jehoshaphat, chief over 300,000 men ([2 Chr. 17:14](#2Chr.17.14)).

The fourth son of David ([2 Sam. 3:4](#2Sam.3.4)). After the death of his elder brothers, Amnon and Absalom, he became heir-apparent to the throne. But Solomon, a younger brother, was preferred to him. Adonijah, however, when his father was dying, caused himself to be proclaimed king. But Nathan and Bathsheba induced David to give orders that Solomon should at once be proclaimed and admitted to the throne. Adonijah fled and took refuge at the altar, and received pardon for his conduct from Solomon on the condition that he showed himself “a worthy man” ([1 Kings 1:5-53](#1Kgs.1.5)). He afterwards made a second attempt to gain the throne, but was seized and put to death ([1 Kings 2:13-25](#1Kgs.2.13)).
A Levite sent with the princes to teach the book of the law to the inhabitants of Judah ([2 Chr. 17:8](#2Chr.17.8)).
One of the “chiefs of the people” after the Captivity ([Neh. 10:16](#Neh.10.16)).
Whom the Lord sets up, one of those “which came with Zerubbabel” ([Ezra 2:13](#Ezra.2.13)). His “children,” or retainers, to the number of 666, came up to Jerusalem (8:13).

One who was “over the tribute;” i.e., “over the levy.” He was stoned by the Israelites after they had revolted from Rehoboam ([2 Chr. 10:18](#2Chr.10.18)). Called also Adoram ([2 Sam. 20:24](#2Sam.20.24)) and Adoniram ([1 Kings 4:6](#1Kgs.4.6)).
A son of Sennacherib, king of Assyria ([2 Kings 19:37](#2Kgs.19.37); [Isa. 37:38](#Isa.37.38)).
An idol; a form of the sun-god worshipped by the inhabitants of Sepharvaim ([2 Kings 17:31](#2Kgs.17.31)), and brought by the Sepharvite colonists into Samaria.

Flock of God, the son of Barzillai, the Meholathite, to whom Saul gave in marriage his daughter Merab ([1 Sam. 18:19](#1Sam.18.19)). The five sons that sprang from this union were put to death by the Gibeonites ([2 Sam. 21:8](#2Sam.21.8), [9](#2Sam.21.9). Here it is said that Michal “brought up” [R.V., “bare”] these five sons, either that she treated them as if she had been their own mother, or that for “Michal” we should read “Merab,” as in [1 Sam. 18:19](#1Sam.18.19)).

A “prophet,” probably one of the seventy disciples of Christ. He prophesied at Antioch of an approaching famine ([Acts 11:27](#Acts.11.27), [28](#Acts.11.28)). Many years afterwards he met Paul at Caesarea, and warned him of the bonds and affliction that awaited him at Jerusalem should he persist in going thither ([Acts 21:10-12](#Acts.21.10)).

Another king of the Amalekites whom Saul spared unlawfully, but whom Samuel on his arrival in the camp of Saul ordered, in retributive justice ([Judg. 1](#Judg.1)), to be brought out and cut in pieces ([1 Sam. 15:8-33](#1Sam.15.8). Comp. [Ex. 17:11](#Exod.17.11); [Num. 14:45](#Num.14.45)).
A king of the Amalekites referred to by Balaam ([Num. 24:7](#Num.24.7)). He lived at the time of the Exodus.
Fugitive, the father of Shammah, who was one of David’s mighty men ([2 Sam. 23:11](#2Sam.23.11))

Son of the foregoing, was born at Rome, A.D. 27. He was the brother of Bernice and Drusilla. The Emperor Claudius (A.D. 48) invested him with the office of superintendent of the Temple of Jerusalem, and made him governor (A.D. 50) of Chalcis. He was afterwards raised to the rank of king, and made governor over the tetrarchy of Philip and Lysanias ([Acts 25:13](#Acts.25.13); [26:2](#Acts.26.2), [7](#Acts.26.7)). It was before him that Paul delivered (A.D. 59) his speech recorded in [Acts 26](#Acts.26). His private life was very profligate. He died (the last of his race) at Rome, at the age of about seventy years, A.D. 100.
Gatherer; the collector, mentioned as author of the sayings in [Prov. 30](#Prov.30). Nothing is known of him beyond what is there recorded.

The son of Omri, whom he succeeded as the seventh king of Israel. His history is recorded in [1 Kings 16](#1Kgs.16)-22. His wife was Jezebel (q.v.), who exercised a very evil influence over him. To the calf-worship introduced by Jeroboam he added the worship of Baal. He was severely admonished by Elijah (q.v.) for his wickedness. His anger was on this account kindled against the prophet, and he sought to kill him. He undertook three campaigns against Ben-hadad II., king of Damascus. …
A false prophet referred to by Jeremiah ([Jer. 29:21](#Jer.29.21)), of whom nothing further is known.

The son of Darius Hystaspes, the king named in the Book of Esther. He ruled over the kingdoms of Persia, Media, and Babylonia, “from India to Ethiopia.” This was in all probability the Xerxes of profane history, who succeeded his father Darius (B.C. 485). In the LXX. version of the Book of Esther the name Artaxerxes occurs for Ahasuerus. He reigned for twenty-one years (B.C. 486-465). He invaded Greece with an army, it is said, of more than 2,000,000 soldiers, only 5,000 of whom returned with him. Leonidas, with his famous 300, arrested his progress at the Pass of Thermopylae, and then he was defeated disastrously by Themistocles at Salamis. It was after his return from this invasion that Esther was chosen as his queen.
The son and successor of Jotham, king of Judah ([2 Kings 16](#2Kgs.16); [Isa. 7](#Isa.7)-9; [2 Chr. 28](#2Chr.28)). He gave himself up to a life of wickedness and idolatry. …

The son of Joram, or Jehoram, and sixth king of Judah. Called Jehoahaz ([2 Chr. 21:17](#2Chr.21.17); [25:23](#2Chr.25.23)), and Azariah ([2 Chr. 22:6](#2Chr.22.6)). Guided by his idolatrous mother Athaliah, his reign was disastrous ([2 Kings 8:24-29](#2Kgs.8.24); [9:29](#2Kgs.9.29)). He joined his uncle Jehoram, king of Israel, in an expedition against Hazael, king of Damascus; but was wounded at the pass of Gur when attempting to escape, and had strength only to reach Megiddo, where he died ([2 Kings 9:22-28](#2Kgs.9.22)). He reigned only one year.

The son and successor of Ahab. He followed the counsels of his mother Jezebel, and imitated in wickedness the ways of his father. In his reign the Moabites revolted from under his authority ([2 Kings 3:5-7](#2Kgs.3.5)). He united with Jehoshaphat in an attempt to revive maritime trade by the Red Sea, which proved a failure ([2 Chr. 20:35-37](#2Chr.20.35)). His messengers, sent to consult the god of Ekron regarding his recovery from the effects of a fall from the roof-gallery of his palace, were met on the way by Elijah, who sent them back to tell the king that he would never rise from his bed ([1 Kings 22:51](#1Kgs.22.51); [2 Kings 1:18](#2Kgs.1.18)).
One of the sons of Bela ([1 Chr. 8:7](#1Chr.8.7), R.V.). In A.V. called “Ahiah.”
Mother’s brother, one of David’s thirty heroes ([2 Sam. 23:33](#2Sam.23.33); [1 Chr. 11:35](#1Chr.11.35)).
The chief of the Benjamite slingers that repaired to David at Ziklag ([1 Chr. 12:3](#1Chr.12.3)).
Name different in Hebrew, meaning brother of Judah. Chief of the tribe of Asher; one of those appointed by Moses to superintend the division of Canaan among the tribe ([Num. 34:27](#Num.34.27)).
A son of Bela, the son of Benjamin ([1 Chr. 8:7](#1Chr.8.7)).

A prophet of Shiloh ([1 Kings 11:29](#1Kgs.11.29); [14:2](#1Kgs.14.2)), called the “Shilonite,” in the days of Rehoboam. We have on record two of his remarkable prophecies, [1 Kings 11:31-39](#1Kgs.11.31), announcing the rending of the ten tribes from Solomon; and [1 Kings 14:6-16](#1Kgs.14.6), delivered to Jeroboam’s wife, foretelling the death of Abijah the king’s son, the destruction of Jeroboam’s house, and the captivity of Israel “beyond the river.” Jeroboam bears testimony to the high esteem in which he was held as a prophet of God ([1 Kings 14:2](#1Kgs.14.2), [3](#1Kgs.14.3)).
One of the five sons of Jerahmeel, who was great-grandson of Judah ([1 Chr. 2:25](#1Chr.2.25)).
A Pelonite, one of David’s heroes ([1 Chr. 11:36](#1Chr.11.36)); called also Eliam ([2 Sam. 23:34](#2Sam.23.34)).
A Levite having charge of the sacred treasury in the temple ([1 Chr. 26:20](#1Chr.26.20)).

Brother of support = helper, one of the five whom Josiah sent to consult the prophetess Huldah in connection with the discovery of the book of the law ([2 Kings 22:12-14](#2Kgs.22.12); [2 Chr. 34:20](#2Chr.34.20)). He was the son of Shaphan, the royal secretary, and the father of Gedaliah, governor of Judea after the destruction of Jerusalem by the Babylonians ([2 Kings 25:22](#2Kgs.25.22); [Jer. 40:5-16](#Jer.40.5); [43:6](#Jer.43.6)). On one occasion he protected Jeremiah against the fury of Jehoiakim ([Jer. 26:24](#Jer.26.24)). It was in the chamber of another son (Germariah) of Shaphan that Baruch read in the ears of all the people Jeremiah’s roll.

The son and successor of Zadok in the office of high priest ([1 Chr. 6:8](#1Chr.6.8), [53](#1Chr.6.53)). On the occasion of the revolt of Absalom he remained faithful to David, and was of service to him in conveying to him tidings of the proceedings of Absalom in Jerusalem ([2 Sam. 15:24-37](#2Sam.15.24); [17:15-21](#2Sam.17.15)). He was swift of foot, and was the first to carry to David tidings of the defeat of Absalom, although he refrained, from delicacy of feeling, from telling him of his death ([2 Sam. 18:19-33](#2Sam.18.19)).
The father Ahinoam, the wife of Saul ([1 Sam. 14:50](#1Sam.14.50)).

One of the three giant Anakim brothers whom Caleb and the spies saw in Mount Hebron ([Num. 13:22](#Num.13.22)) when they went in to explore the land. They were afterwards driven out and slain ([Josh. 15:14](#Josh.15.14); [Judg. 1:10](#Judg.1.10)).
One of the guardians of the temple after the Exile ([1 Chr. 9:17](#1Chr.9.17)).

Son of Ahitub ([1 Sam. 14:3](#1Sam.14.3), [18](#1Sam.14.18)), Ichabod’s brother; the same probably as Ahimelech, who was high priest at Nob in the reign of Saul ([1 Sam. 22:11](#1Sam.22.11)). Some, however, suppose that Ahimelech was the brother of Ahijah, and that they both officiated as high priests, Ahijah at Gibeah or Kirjath-jearim, and Ahimelech at Nob.

The son of Abiathar, and high priest in the time of David ([1 Chr. 18:16](#1Chr.18.16)). In the parallel passage, [2 Sam. 8:17](#2Sam.8.17), we have the name Ahimelech, and Abiathar, the son of Ahimelech. This most authorities consider the more correct reading.

Brother of liberality = liberal, one of the twelve commissariat officers appointed by Solomon in so many districts of his kingdom to raise supplies by monthly rotation for his household. He was appointed to the district of Mahanaim ([1 Kings 4:14](#1Kgs.4.14)), east of Jordan.

A Jezreelitess, the first wife of David ([1 Sam. 25:43](#1Sam.25.43); [27:3](#1Sam.27.3)). She was the mother of Amnon ([2 Sam. 3:2](#2Sam.3.2)). (See [1 Sam. 30:5](#1Sam.30.5), [18](#1Sam.30.18); [2 Sam. 2:2](#2Sam.2.2).)
The daughter of Ahimaaz, and wife of Saul ([1 Sam. 14:50](#1Sam.14.50)).

One of the sons of Abinadab the Levite. While Uzzah went by the side of the ark, he walked before it guiding the oxen which drew the cart on which it was carried, after having brought it from his father’s house in Gibeah ([1 Chr. 13:7](#1Chr.13.7); [2 Sam. 6:3](#2Sam.6.3), [4](#2Sam.6.4)).
One of the sons of Jehiel the Gibeonite ([1 Chr. 8:31](#1Chr.8.31); [9:37](#1Chr.9.37)).
One of the sons of Beriah ([1 Chr. 8:14](#1Chr.8.14)).
Brother of evil = unlucky, or my brother is friend, chief of the tribe of Naphtali at the Exodus ([Num. 1:15](#Num.1.15); [2:29](#Num.2.29)).
Brother of song = singer, the officer who was “over the household” of Solomon ([1 Kings 4:6](#1Kgs.4.6)).

Brother of insipidity or impiety, a man greatly renowned for his sagacity among the Jews. At the time of Absalom’s revolt he deserted David ([Ps. 41:9](#Ps.41.9); [55:12-14](#Ps.55.12)) and espoused the cause of Absalom ([2 Sam. 15:12](#2Sam.15.12)). David sent his old friend Hushai back to Absalom, in order that he might counteract the counsel of Ahithophel ([2 Sam. 15:31-37](#2Sam.15.31)). This end was so far gained that Ahithophel saw he had no longer any influence, and accordingly he at once left the camp of Absalom and returned to Giloh, his native place, where, after arranging his wordly affairs, he hanged himself, and was buried in the sepulchre of his fathers ([2 Sam. 17:1-23](#2Sam.17.1)). He was the type of Judas ([Ps. 41:9](#Ps.41.9)).

The son of Phinehas. On the death of his grandfather Eli he succeeded to the office of high priest, and was himself succeeded by his son Ahijah ([1 Sam. 14:3](#1Sam.14.3); [22:9](#1Sam.22.9), [11](#1Sam.22.11), [12](#1Sam.22.12), [20](#1Sam.22.20)).
The father of Zadok, who was made high priest by Saul after the extermination of the family of Ahimelech ([1 Chr. 6:7](#1Chr.6.7), [8](#1Chr.6.8); [2 Sam. 8:17](#2Sam.8.17)).

Brotherly, one of the sons of Bela, the son of Benjamin ([1 Chr. 8:4](#1Chr.8.4)). He is also called Ahiah (ver. 7) and Iri ([1 Chr. 7:7](#1Chr.7.7)). His descendants were called Ahohites ([2 Sam. 23:9](#2Sam.23.9), [28](#2Sam.23.28)).

Tent of the father, an artist of the tribe of Dan, appointed to the work of preparing materials for the tabernacle ([Ex. 31:6](#Exod.31.6); [35:34](#Exod.35.34); [36:1](#Exod.36.1), [2](#Exod.36.2); [38:23](#Exod.38.23)).

My tent is in her, the name of an imaginary harlot, applied symbolically to Jerusalem, because she had abandoned the worship of the true God and given herself up to the idolatries of foreign nations. ([Ezek. 23:4](#Ezek.23.4), [11](#Ezek.23.11), [22](#Ezek.23.22), [36](#Ezek.23.36), [44](#Ezek.23.44)).
Jewess, the daughter of Beeri the Hittite, and one of Esau’s wives ([Gen. 26:34](#Gen.26.34)), elsewhere called Aholibamah (36:2-14).
He twists, one of the sons of Ezer, the son of Seir the Horite ([1 Chr. 1:42](#1Chr.1.42)).
A Levite who kept the gate of the temple after the return from Babylon ([1 Chr. 9:17](#1Chr.9.17); [Ezra 2:42](#Ezra.2.42); [Neh. 7:45](#Neh.7.45)).
The head of one of the families of Nethinim ([Ezra 2:45](#Ezra.2.45)).
One of the nine sons of Becher, the son of Benjamin ([1 Chr. 7:8](#1Chr.7.8)).
One of the sons of Jehoadah, or Jarah, son of Ahaz ([1 Chr. 8:36](#1Chr.8.36)).

A coppersmith who, with Hymenaeus and others, promulgated certain heresies regarding the resurrection ([1 Tim. 1:19](#1Tim.1.19); [2 Tim. 4:14](#2Tim.4.14)), and made shipwreck of faith and of a good conscience. Paul excommunicated him ([1 Tim. 1:20](#1Tim.1.20); comp. [1 Cor. 5:5](#1Cor.5.5)).
A man whose father, Simon the Cyrenian, bore the cross of Christ ([Mark 15:21](#Mark.15.21)).
A relative of Annas the high priest, present when Peter and John were examined before the Sanhedrim ([Acts 4:6](#Acts.4.6)).

A Jew of Ephesus who took a prominent part in the uproar raised there by the preaching of Paul ([Acts 19:33](#Acts.19.33)). The Jews put him forward to plead their cause before the mob. It was probably intended that he should show that he and the other Jews had no sympathy with Paul any more than the Ephesians had. It is possible that this man was the same as the following.
The son of Jedaiah, of the family of the Simeonites, who expelled the Hamites from the valley of Gedor ([1 Chr. 4:37](#1Chr.4.37)).
Immeasurable, the first named of the sons of Joktan ([Gen. 10:26](#Gen.10.26)), the founder of an Arabian tribe.

The father of James the Less, the apostle and writer of the epistle ([Matt. 10:3](#Matt.10.3); [Mark 3:18](#Mark.3.18); [Luke 6:15](#Luke.6.15); [Acts 1:13](#Acts.1.13)), and the husband of Mary ([John 19:25](#John.19.25)). The Hebrew form of this name is Cleopas, or Clopas (q.v.).
The father of Levi, or Matthew ([Mark 2:14](#Mark.2.14)).

Dweller in a valley, the son of Eliphaz and grandson of Esau ([Gen. 36:12](#Gen.36.12); [1 Chr. 1:36](#1Chr.1.36)); the chief of an Idumean tribe ([Gen. 36:16](#Gen.36.16)). His mother was a Horite, a tribe whose territory the descendants of Esau had seized.

One of the descendants of Aaron by Eleazar ([1 Chr. 6:7](#1Chr.6.7), [52](#1Chr.6.52)). He was probably the last of the high priests of Eleazar’s line prior to the transfer of that office to Eli, of the line of Ithamar.
A Levite, son of Hebron, of the lineage of Moses ([1 Chr. 23:19](#1Chr.23.19); [24:23](#1Chr.24.23)).
A “chief priest” who took an active part in the reformation under Jehoshaphat ([2 Chr. 19:11](#2Chr.19.11)); probably the same as mentioned in [1 Chr. 6:9](#1Chr.6.9).
One of the high priests in the time of Hezekiah ([2 Chr. 31:15](#2Chr.31.15)).

The son of Abigail, a sister of king David ([1 Chr. 2:17](#1Chr.2.17); [2 Sam. 17:25](#2Sam.17.25)). He was appointed by David to command the army in room of his cousin Joab ([2 Sam. 19:13](#2Sam.19.13)), who afterwards treacherously put him to death as a dangerous rival ([2 Sam. 20:4-12](#2Sam.20.4)).
A son of Hadlai, and chief of Ephraim ([2 Chr. 28:12](#2Chr.28.12)) in the reign of Ahaz.
A Levite, son of Elkanah, of the ancestry of Samuel ([1 Chr. 6:25](#1Chr.6.25), [35](#1Chr.6.35)).
The leader of a body of men who joined David in the “stronghold,” probably of Adullam ([1 Chr. 12:18](#1Chr.12.18)).
One of the priests appointed to precede the ark with blowing of trumpets on its removal from the house of Obed-edom ([1 Chr. 15:24](#1Chr.15.24)).
The father of a Levite, one of the two Kohathites who took a prominent part at the instance of Hezekiah in the cleansing of the temple ([2 Chr. 29:12](#2Chr.29.12)).

Burden of (i.e., “sustained by”) Jehovah, the “son of Zichri, who willingly offered himself unto the Lord,” a captain over thousands under Jehoshaphat ([2 Chr. 17:16](#2Chr.17.16); comp. [Judg. 5:9](#Judg.5.9)).

The son and successor of Joash, and eighth king of the separate kingdom of Judah ([2 Kings 14:1-4](#2Kgs.14.1)). He began his reign by punishing the murderers of his father (5-7; [2 Chr. 25:3-5](#2Chr.25.3)). He was the first to employ a mercenary army of 100,000 Israelite soldiers, which he did in his attempt to bring the Edomites again under the yoke of Judah ([2 Chr. 25:5](#2Chr.25.5), [6](#2Chr.25.6)). He was commanded by a prophet of the Lord to send back the mercenaries, which he did ([2 Chr. 25:7-10](#2Chr.25.7), [13](#2Chr.25.13)), much to their annoyance. …
A priest of the golden calves at Bethel ([Amos 7:10-17](#Amos.7.10)).
The father of Joshah, one of the Simeonite chiefs in the time of Hezekiah ([1 Chr. 4:34](#1Chr.4.34)).
A Levite, son of Hilkiah, of the descendants of Ethan the Merarite ([1 Chr. 6:45](#1Chr.6.45)).
True, the father of Jonah the prophet, a native of Gath-hepher ([2 Kings 14:25](#2Kgs.14.25); [Jonah 1:1](#Jonah.1.1)).
The father of Machir of Lo-debar, in whose house Mephibosheth resided ([2 Sam. 9:4](#2Sam.9.4), [5](#2Sam.9.5); 17:27).

One of the twelve spies sent by Moses to search the land of Canaan ([Num. 13:12](#Num.13.12)). He was one of the ten who perished by the plague for their unfavourable report ([Num. 14:37](#Num.14.37)).
One of the sons of Obed-edom the Levite ([1 Chr. 26:5](#1Chr.26.5)).
The father of the Ephraimite chief Elishama, at the time of the Exodus ([Num. 1:10](#Num.1.10); [2:18](#Num.2.18); [7:48](#Num.7.48), [53](#Num.7.53)).
The father of Talmai, king of Geshur, to whom Absalom fled after the murder of Amnon ([2 Sam. 13:37](#2Sam.13.37)).
The son of Omri, and the father of Uthai ([1 Chr. 9:4](#1Chr.9.4)).

The father of Nahshon, who was chief of the tribe of Judah ([Num. 1:7](#Num.1.7); [2:3](#Num.2.3); [7:12](#Num.7.12), [17](#Num.7.17); [10:14](#Num.10.14)). His daughter Elisheba was married to Aaron ([Ex. 6:23](#Exod.6.23)).
Chief of the 112 descendants of Uzziel the Levite ([1 Chr. 15:10](#1Chr.15.10), [11](#1Chr.15.11)).

People of the Almighty, the father of Ahiezer, who was chief of the Danites at the time of the Exodus ([Num. 1:12](#Num.1.12); [2:25](#Num.2.25)). This is one of the few names compounded with the name of God, Shaddai, “Almighty.”
People of the giver, the son of Benaiah, who was the third and chief captain of the host under David ([1 Chr. 27:6](#1Chr.27.6)).

The eldest son of David, by Ahinoam of Jezreel ([1 Chr. 3:1](#1Chr.3.1); [2 Sam. 3:2](#2Sam.3.2)). Absalom caused him to be put to death for his great crime in the matter of Tamar ([2 Sam. 13:28](#2Sam.13.28), [29](#2Sam.13.29)).
One of the sons of Shammai, of the children of Ezra ([1 Chr. 4:20](#1Chr.4.20); comp. 17).

The son of Manasseh, and fourteenth king of Judah. He restored idolatry, and set up the images which his father had cast down. Zephaniah (1:4; 3:4, 11) refers to the moral depravity prevailing in this king’s reign.
The governor of Samaria in the time of Ahab. The prophet Micaiah was committed to his custody ([1 Kings 22:26](#1Kgs.22.26); [2 Chr. 18:25](#2Chr.18.25)).
Highlanders, or hillmen, the name given to the descendants of one of the sons of Canaan ([Gen. 14:7](#Gen.14.7)), called Amurra or Amurri in the Assyrian and Egyptian inscriptions. …

Borne; a burden, one of the twelve minor prophets. He was a native of Tekota, the modern Tekua, a town about 12 miles south-east of Bethlehem. He was a man of humble birth, neither a “prophet nor a prophet’s son,” but “an herdman and a dresser of sycomore trees,” R.V. He prophesied in the days of Uzziah, king of Judah, and was contemporary with Isaiah and Hosea ([Amos 1:1](#Amos.1.1); [7:14](#Amos.7.14), [15](#Amos.7.15); [Zech. 14:5](#Zech.14.5)), who survived him a few years. Under Jeroboam II. the kingdom of Israel rose to the zenith of its prosperity; but that was followed by the prevalence of luxury and vice and idolatry. At this period Amos was called from his obscurity to remind the people of the law of God’s retributive justice, and to call them to repentance.

Strong, the father of the prophet Isaiah ([2 Kings 19:2](#2Kgs.19.2), [20](#2Kgs.19.20); 20:1; [Isa. 1:1](#Isa.1.1); [2:1](#Isa.2.1)). As to his personal history little is positively known. He is supposed by some to have been the “man of God” spoken of in [2 Chr. 25:7](#2Chr.25.7), [8](#2Chr.25.8).
A Roman Christian saluted by Paul ([Rom. 16:8](#Rom.16.8)).

The son of Kohath, the son of Levi. He married Jochebed, “his father’s sister,” and was the father of Aaron, Miriam, and Moses ([Ex. 6:18](#Exod.6.18), [20](#Exod.6.20); [Num. 3:19](#Num.3.19)). He died in Egypt at the age of 137 years ([Ex. 6:20](#Exod.6.20)). His descendants were called Amramites ([Num. 3:27](#Num.3.27); [1 Chr. 26:23](#1Chr.26.23)).

King of Shinar, southern Chaldea, one of the confederates of Chedorlaomer, king of Elam, in a war against Sodom and cities of the plain ([Gen. 14:1](#Gen.14.1), [4](#Gen.14.4)). It is now found that Amraphel (or Ammirapaltu) is the Khammu-rabi whose name appears on recently-discovered monuments. After defeating Arioch (q.v.) he united Babylonia under one rule, and made Babylon his capital.
Long-necked, the son of Arba, father of the Anakim ([Josh. 15:13](#Josh.15.13); [21:11](#Josh.21.11), Heb. Anok).
The name of an Egyptian tribe descended from Mizraim ([Gen. 10:13](#Gen.10.13); [1 Chr. 1:11](#1Chr.1.11)).

One of the gods worshipped by the people of Sepharvaim, who colonized Samaria ([2 Kings 17:31](#2Kgs.17.31)). The name means “Anu is king.” It was a female deity representing the moon, as Adrammelech (q.v.) was the male representing the sun.
Cloud, one of the Israelites who sealed the covenant after the return from Babylon ([Neh. 10:26](#Neh.10.26)).
